title: Offshore Installation and Marine Operations
analyses: Heavy lifting and crane capacity analysis
Lift rigging and sling load analysis
Pipeline, cable and umbilical laying analysis
scope: Applicable to jacket, topside, subsea equipment, wind foundation, pipeline, cable and floating structure installations.

models.text: The suite should implement Newton's laws of motion, rigid-body equilibrium, conservation of linear and angular momentum, Newton–Euler equations, Lagrange's equations, d'Alembert's principle, energy conservation, buoyancy equilibrium, cable tension relationships, nonlinear lifting equilibrium and structural finite-element analysis.

The suite should include multibody lifting dynamics, sling force distribution, nonlinear cable and sling stiffness, elastic spreader-beam analysis, crane load-radius models, dynamic amplification, pendulum motion, hook-load dynamics, lifting-point stress assessment, nonlinear rigging contact and vessel-motion-induced lifted-load response.

The suite should implement Archimedes' buoyancy principle, hydrostatic restoring, metacentric stability, righting-arm calculations, six-degree-of-freedom vessel dynamics, potential-flow radiation and diffraction, response amplitude operators, Cummins' impulse response equation, wave drift forces, added-mass models and viscous hydrodynamic damping.

The suite should include rigid-body load transfer, skid friction models, support reaction redistribution, structural grillage analysis, beam and plate bending, transportation inertia forces, nonlinear seafastening restraints, cargo support contact and fatigue under repeated vessel motions.

The suite should include time-varying buoyancy, nonlinear rigid-body rotational dynamics, jacket launching trajectory models, rocker-arm load transfer, launch cradle friction, hydrostatic equilibrium, added-mass effects, hydrodynamic damping and controlled flooding models.

models.group: Pipeline, cable and umbilical installation models
models.text: The suite should incorporate nonlinear catenary equations, rod and cable finite elements, overbend and sagbend analysis, tensioner stiffness models, seabed touchdown contact, hydrodynamic loading, minimum bend radius and deployment transient simulation.

models.group: Splash-zone lowering and subsea landing models
models.text: Applicable approaches include Morison wave-current loading, added mass, time-varying buoyancy, slamming impact models, nonlinear lowering-line dynamics, vessel heave coupling, contact-impact mechanics and seabed touchdown response.

models.group: Pile driving and suction foundation installation
models.text: The suite should include one-dimensional pile stress-wave propagation, Smith-type pile driving analysis, hammer–pile–soil interaction, dynamic soil resistance models, shaft friction, toe resistance, undrained soil strength models, soil seepage, suction penetration resistance, effective stress analysis and nonlinear soil–structure interaction.

The suite should implement nonlinear vessel motions, ballast-induced displacement variation, hydrostatic equilibrium, leg mating unit stiffness and damping, nonlinear contact, impact response, mechanical load transfer and time-domain coupled structural analysis.

The suite should include wave scatter statistics, Markov-chain weather modelling, persistence probability models, Monte Carlo simulation, extreme value statistics, Weibull distributions, generalized extreme value distributions, weather downtime models and probabilistic installation schedule assessment.

The suite should integrate nonlinear structural removal analysis, temporary load redistribution, dynamic lifting, damaged-structure finite elements, corrosion-informed residual strength, vessel hydrodynamics, stochastic weather windows and operation sequencing. Hybrid frameworks should couple marine operation dynamics with structural strength, geotechnical resistance, equipment limits and probabilistic schedule risk.

subtitle: Heavy lifting, load-out, transportation, tow-out, launching, upending, laying, lowering, float-over, installation weather windows and decommissioning.
ic: The initial conditions shall establish the configuration of the installation object, installation vessel, crane, rigging system, transportation supports and surrounding marine environment at the selected operation stage.

The object shall initially have a specified position, orientation, weight, centre of gravity and structural stress state. For lifting operations, the initial state may be the object resting on temporary supports or already suspended in equilibrium with rigging tension.

Load-out simulations shall begin with the structure supported by its initial skidway, trailers or transport arrangement, including support reactions and contact conditions. Transportation simulations shall initialize cargo support, seafastening, vessel draft, ballast and intact stability.

Jacket launching studies shall establish the initial position on the launch barge, support contact, initial rotation and buoyancy characteristics. Upending simulations shall initialize the partially submerged structure, flooding state, buoyancy distribution and connection to lifting equipment.

Subsea lowering studies shall establish suspended length, object elevation, cable tension, lowering velocity and environmental conditions. Float-over operations shall initialize the transport vessel position, draft, trim, relative alignment and deck support clearance.
Decommissioning simulations shall start from the actual structural condition, including corrosion, residual loading, damaged members and the prescribed dismantling stage.
bc: Crane and lifting boundaries shall prescribe hook support, crane radius, boom geometry, sling connections, lifting-point reactions and allowable crane motion. Where dynamic lifting is modelled, vessel or crane motions shall be imposed or solved in a coupled manner.

Load-out boundaries shall represent skidway support, friction, trailer contact, quay support, pulling forces and evolving load-transfer conditions. Transportation boundaries shall apply seafastening restraints, vessel accelerations and environmental loads.
Towing boundaries shall prescribe towline connections, towing forces, tow vessel motion, hydrodynamic drag and relevant towline elasticity.

Launching and upending analyses shall allow evolving contact, water entry, buoyancy changes and prescribed or dynamically calculated lifting forces. Subsea landing analyses shall apply lowering motion, hydrodynamic forces and progressive seabed contact.

Pile installation boundaries shall represent hammer loading, pile penetration and soil resistance. Suction-bucket installation shall prescribe pumping pressure differences and soil contact resistance.

For float-over operations, vessel motions, ballast transfers, support contact and mating clearances shall be imposed or coupled as necessary. Weather-window assessments shall use operational thresholds for wind, waves, current and the required continuous operation duration.

calibration: Calibration should use recorded offshore installation operations, crane load-cell measurements, vessel motion monitoring, load-out records, transportation accelerometer measurements and marine equipment performance tests.
Crane load response and dynamic amplification parameters should be calibrated against instrumented lifting trials and manufacturer-certified crane performance data.
Rigging stiffness, load sharing and friction characteristics should be calibrated using sling tests, spreader beam measurements and instrumented lifting arrangements.
Load-out models should be calibrated using measured skidway friction, hydraulic jack loads, trailer reactions and recorded structural movements.
Transportation response should be calibrated using vessel motion measurements, sea state observations, cargo accelerations and measured seafastening forces where available.
Jacket launching and upending models should be calibrated against recorded launch motions, buoyancy changes, ballast operations, lifting tensions and measured rotation histories.
Dynamic lowering and splash-zone models should use wave-basin experiments, submerged body hydrodynamic tests and instrumented offshore lowering operations.
Pile driving models should be calibrated using hammer performance measurements, recorded blow counts, pile penetration histories and site-specific soil measurements.
Suction foundation installation models should be calibrated using measured suction pressure, penetration depth, pump performance and seabed soil response.
Float-over simulations should use measured vessel motion, ballast response and mating reaction data from representative operations.
Weather-window and operability models should be calibrated using historical environmental observations, actual offshore operation durations and documented weather-related interruptions.
verification: Lifting and rigging calculations should be verified through analytical force equilibrium, sling load distribution, known lifting configurations and independently calculated crane loading cases.
Dynamic lifting calculations should undergo time-step convergence and checks of inertia, damping, hydrodynamic force and vessel motion input implementation.
Load-out and skidway calculations should be verified against prescribed sliding, friction and support-transfer benchmarks.
Transportation analyses should be tested for consistent application of vessel accelerations, cargo inertia, seafastening reactions and support conditions.
Launching and upending models should be checked for correct buoyancy, centre-of-gravity movement, rotational equilibrium and transition between installation stages.
Lowering simulations should undergo convergence testing for line tension, hydrodynamic loading, splash-zone transitions and landing response.
Pile driving calculations should be verified using prescribed pile resistance and wave-propagation benchmarks appropriate to the selected method.
Suction penetration calculations should be checked against independently calculated geotechnical reference cases and consistent pressure-force accounting.
Float-over simulations should undergo clearance, contact, motion and support-transfer verification.
Weather-window calculations should be checked against independently analysed environmental time series, with explicit testing of the duration and threshold logic.
Decommissioning calculations should be subjected to lifting, load redistribution, structural stability and removal-sequence benchmark checks.
validation: Crane loads, sling tensions and lifted-object motions should be compared with independent lifting trial data and monitored offshore operations.
Load-out forces, skid movement and temporary support reactions should be validated using actual load-out measurements.
Transportation predictions should be assessed against measured vessel accelerations, seafastening loads and recorded structural response.
Jacket launching and upending predictions should be compared with actual installation trajectories and instrumented operations.
Subsea lowering and landing predictions should be evaluated against recorded wire tensions, deployment motions, landing velocities and touchdown measurements.
Pile driving resistance and penetration predictions should be assessed using independent pile installation records.
Suction foundation installation predictions should be compared with measured suction pressure, penetration rate and observed installation behaviour.
Float-over analyses should be evaluated using mating load records, measured clearances, ballast histories and vessel motion measurements.
Weather-window models should be evaluated by comparing predicted operability with historical marine operations, including delays and actual environmental conditions.
Decommissioning models should be assessed against documented removal operations, measured lifting loads and observed structural responses.

geometry.text: Heavy lifting arrangements, crane vessels, transport barges, jacket launching systems, skidways, seafastening structures, towing configurations, pipeline-laying systems, subsea lowering arrangements, float-over installations and decommissioning assemblies.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, IFC, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for installation structures, crane components, lifted modules, jackets, lifting frames, vessel decks, skidways, transportation supports and temporary structural assemblies.

geometry.cat: Ship, barge and installation-vessel geometry formats
geometry.text: NURBS hull-surface representations, IGES hull geometry, STEP hull assemblies, offset tables in CSV or JSON, DXF hull sections and documented marine hull-surface formats should be supported. The imported vessel model should preserve hull geometry, deck geometry, lifting equipment positions, ballast compartment boundaries and relevant loading interfaces.

Structured CSV, XML and JSON geometry descriptions should be accepted for lifting points, sling endpoints, spreader bars, rigging connections, crane positions, load-out support coordinates, towline paths, launching trajectories and installation stages. These are custom engineering data schemas, not universally standardized CAD exchange formats.

Nastran BDF, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU, Exodus, CGNS, SU2, OpenFOAM polyMesh and supported hydrodynamic panel meshes should be accepted for appropriate structural, vessel-response, splash-zone, impact and fluid–structure interaction analyses.

GeoTIFF, LandXML, InfraGML, GeoJSON, GML, GeoPackage, Shapefile, ESRI ASCII Grid, XYZ bathymetry and LAS/LAZ should be supported for marine routes, offshore installation locations, foundation positions, pipeline corridors, seabed obstructions and port infrastructure.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, 3MF, E57, point-cloud-derived models and photogrammetric meshes should be accepted for legacy installation equipment, existing vessels, site surveys, damaged equipment and complex lifted-object geometries.
